newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Products Outlook - Gulf gasoline remains tight.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Products Outlook - Gulf gasoline remains tight.

text.p: An unusual flipflop in prices for conventional unleaded gasoline, with Gulf Coast barrels recently fetching near or more than New York Harbor, is expected to preoccupy many oil products players early this week, observers said.

Traders said short-term tightness in Gulf supply, aggravated by a spate of Gulf Coast refinery outages, has helped Gulf Coast M4-grade gasoline command exceptionally firm prices vis-a-vis New York Harbor in the past week.

"It's been a real surprising move," said Dean Witter energy analyst Steve Platt, who attributed the Gulf price move to "concerted cash buying by majors on talk about turnarounds and refinery problems."

New York prices usually trend 2.0 to 2.5 cents a gallon higher than the Gulf Coast because it costs about that much per gallon to ship fuel north on the Colonial Pipeline from "Refinery Row" in Texas to New York Harbor .

Spot New York M4-grade was offered Monday at 1.40 cents above December futures, about a half cent more than prompt 32nd cycle Gulf Coast material, traders said, just one fourth its customary premium over southern barrels.
Gulf prices last Wednesday were selling for 73.25 cents a gallon -- a spectacular five cents more than New York and the highest Houston prices since the Mideast Gulf War.
The last time a price flipflop had been seen was May 25, when Gulf prices edged 1.4 cents higher than New York.
Although the Gulf premium vanished by Friday, its price relative to New York remains strong enough to discourage shipments north, some traders said.
"You'll probably see supply congregate in the Gulf and probably tighten in New York Harbor," Platt said. "Why push it up north when there's no incentive to ship it up the Colonial?"

"There's a litany of Who's Who that have been buying in the Gulf," one Texas trader said, noting market talk that Citgo, Exxon and Amoco were among majors snapping up big volumes last week amid a host of refinery disruptions.
"Refiners are buying because they're having short-term supply problems and demand is bloody high," he said.

But the trader predicted U.S. gasoline stocks would swell by as much as four million barrels in tomorrow's weekly estimates by the American Petroleum Institute, with ramped-up production helping restore New York and Gulf differentials to their relative norm.
To be sure, the API estimated daily production of 7.6 million barrels per day (bdy) for the week ending Oct 25, about 363,000 bpd more than the prior week.
Continuing refinery problems, however, could limit stock builds, other traders cautioned, noting the following situations:

* Texas regulators confirmed Oct. 28 that a valve failure had disrupted a fluid catalytic cracker at Amoco Corp's 433,000 bpd refinery in Texas City, Texas. The company, which has declined comment, was seen making large purchases in the Gulf last week.

* Amerada Hess Corp said Friday it has taken down the 110,000 bpd cat cracker at its giant St. Croix refinery in the U.S. Virgin Islands for a four-to-six week upgrade that will increase its capacity to 125,000 bpd.
* Star Enterprise announced previously it would shut down one of two crude units at its 225,000 bpd refinery in Convent, La., beginning Nov 1 for a 20-day repair.

The company, a 50-50 joint venture between Texaco and Saudi Aramco, also said previously it would shut a 15,000 bpd hydrocracker at its 235,000 bpd refinery in Port Arthur, Texas, for an unplanned repair.
* Sun Co Inc said Friday it plans to keep shut the 80,000 bpd crude distillation unit at its refinery in Marcus Hook, Penn., until mid-November for economic reasons.
Original plans had been to shut the crude unit for only 18 days beginning Oct 4 for scheduled maintenance -- coinciding with a 44-day turnaround of the refinery's 85,000 bpd catalytic cracking unit.

* Clark Refining & Marketing has been compelled by a judge to keep two units at its Blue Island, Illinois, refinery shut until a Nov 8 ruling is reached on whether to close the plant completly on safety grounds.

The loss of the propane scrubber and an alkylation unit, in turn, forced the shutdown of the refinery's fluid catalytic cracking unit, leaving the plant running at 55,000 barrels per day compared with its capacity of about 80,000 bpd.
-- New York Energy Desk, 212 859-1632
